headline: Missouri hemp THC law takes effect 12 November after court win
dek: Missouri's Intoxicating Cannabinoid Control Act starts 12 November, moving THCA flower and THC edibles into a licensed system a judge says has no licenses left.
key_points: Missouri's HB 2641, now section 195.900 of state law, takes effect 12 November and treats covered hemp-derived THC products as marijuana that only state-licensed businesses may make or sell.
A federal judge dismissed the hemp industry's challenge on 4 November, calling it premature and noting that no marijuana licenses remain for the state to give out.
Attorney General Catherine Hanaway sued four shops the same day and says more lawsuits will follow once the law is in force.
The state date lands on the same day federal hemp status ends for cannabinoids the plant cannot make; the broader federal 0.4 mg cap follows on 11 December.
body: Missouri's new restrictions on intoxicating hemp products take effect on Thursday, 12 November 2026, after a federal judge threw out the industry's attempt to block them. From that day, THCA flower, THC-infused edibles above natural plant levels and anything made with synthetic cannabinoids are treated as marijuana under state law, and only businesses licensed in Missouri's adult-use and medical marijuana system may grow, make, test, move or sell them.

The switch is the first comprehensive limit on intoxicating hemp in the state. It arrives with enforcement already under way: Attorney General Catherine Hanaway sued four retailers on 4 November, and has told reporters that her office will file more cases once the law is in force. For smoke shops and convenience stores that built a business on hemp-derived THC, the practical question is no longer whether the law survives in court, but how fast the state moves against them.
## What the law changes

House Bill 2641 is now section 195.900 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri, which calls itself the Intoxicating Cannabinoid Control Act. It redefines hemp by total THC, counting THCA as well as delta-9, at no more than 0.3% on a dry-weight basis. Finished hemp-derived products lose hemp status if they contain cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce, natural cannabinoids synthesized outside the plant, or more than 0.4 milligrams of combined THC per container, according to the statute text published by the Missouri Revisor of Statutes.

Anything that falls outside that definition becomes a hemp-derived cannabinoid product, and the law says such products are marijuana under Article XIV of the Missouri Constitution, the voter-approved amendment that created the licensed market. Cultivation, manufacturing, testing, transport and retail sale must happen only inside licensed comprehensive, medical or microbusiness facilities. The statute also bars any seller that is not a licensed dispensary from using the word dispensary, or anything similar, in its business name.

Not every product leaves shelves at once. The hemp trade group USAHAA, which opposes the law, reads the statute as covering three categories from 12 November: smokable or vapeable flower with any THCA, solid edibles with delta-9 above the plant's natural levels, and synthetic cannabinoids. Other hemp THC products, including drinks, are tied to the federal timetable and can stay on sale until 11 December, though not to anyone under 21, according to USAHAA and the Missouri Independent. USAHAA says a violation carries a $5,000 fine per transaction and is a class D felony.
> Missouri has not banned these products so much as handed them to a licensed market that, by the court's own account, is closed to newcomers.
## The court fight ends, for now

The MoHemp Trade Association, Wisconsin drinks maker Lifted Liquids and St. Louis-based MNG 2005, parent of 55 CBD Kratom stores, sued Gov. Mike Kehoe and other officials in July in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri. They argued the law was vague, discriminated against out-of-state companies and was preempted by the 2018 Farm Bill.

Senior District Judge M. Douglas Harpool rejected all three claims in an 18-page order on 4 November, according to USAHAA's summary of the ruling and reporting by the Missouri Independent. He found the law was not preempted, was not vague on its face, and that the plaintiffs lacked standing on the commerce claim. Much of the order turned on timing: because the state had not yet enforced the law against anyone, the challenge was premature. The judge also noted that the health department has no licenses left to issue, a limit he said applies equally to in-state and out-of-state sellers.

That point matters more than the legal holding. A hemp retailer that wants to keep selling THCA flower cannot simply apply for a marijuana licence. Its options are to stop, to partner with a licensee, or to fight on. MNG's compliance manager, Craig Katz, told the Missouri Independent that the plaintiffs are weighing an appeal and will watch how the state enforces the law after 12 November. An appeal would go to the Eighth Circuit.
## Enforcement started before the law did

Hanaway did not wait. On 4 November her office filed civil suits in state circuit courts against Puffers Choice in Aurora, CBD Kratom Cannabis Dispensary in Des Peres, Herb Depot in Independence and Token THC Dispensary in Rock Port, as we reported on 6 November. The state alleges the shops sold products over the legal THC limit as hemp and presented themselves as licensed dispensaries. It seeks civil penalties, injunctions and restitution, and asks courts to declare three of the stores drug-den public nuisances, KY3 reported. None of the allegations has been proven.

The Des Peres case shows the method. Investigators bought two hemp flower products on 8 October and sent them to a state-licensed lab. One label claimed 0.28% delta-9 THC; the lab result cited in the suit was about 4%, more than ten times the hemp limit, according to the Missouri Independent. Hanaway told the paper that after 12 November her office will have more tools and that the new law is easier to enforce.

The scale of possible enforcement is large on paper. The health department previously estimated that about 40,000 food establishments and smoke shops and 1,800 food manufacturers could be affected, though it said most were at low risk of needing investigation. Some hemp sellers planned to protest at the Capitol on Veterans Day, 11 November; a request to burn products on the steps was refused because open flames are not allowed on Capitol grounds.
## Two clocks: state and federal

Missouri's date is not a coincidence of the calendar. The federal law signed on 12 November 2025 redefined hemp nationally on a one-year runway. A stopgap funding bill signed on 2 September 2026 pushed most of it to 11 December, but kept the original date for one piece: from 12 November, products containing cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce lose federal hemp status, according to the Hemp Law Group's tracker. The 0.4 mg per-container cap and the total-THC test arrive federally on 11 December, unless Congress acts first. The FDA still has not published the cannabinoid lists the law required by 10 February, as we reported on 9 November.

Shop owners elsewhere describe the same squeeze. In Durham, North Carolina, one hemp retailer told ABC11 he cannot extend his lease or make large purchases while the December date hangs over the business. Illinois' own Hemp Act also takes effect 12 November; the state agreed not to enforce it against about 250 businesses suing it until a federal hearing on 19 November, as we reported on 10 November, but every other Illinois seller must comply from Thursday.
## Who gains

The licensed side of Missouri's market is not small. Licensed marijuana sales reached about $134.1 million in October, sixth among the states tracked by The Marijuana Herald and only about $3 million behind Illinois. Licensed operators lobbied for a hemp crackdown for years, and some hemp sellers call the law market protection. If intoxicating hemp demand moves to dispensaries rather than to unlicensed sellers, Missouri's monthly totals are the place it should show first, starting with December's figures.
## What to watch

The first post-12 November lawsuits from the attorney general's office will show whether the state targets flower sellers first, as the four existing suits suggest. A notice of appeal from the plaintiffs to the Eighth Circuit would reopen the court fight. On 11 December, the rest of Missouri's law and the federal per-container cap take effect together, which would take most hemp THC drinks off shelves nationwide unless Congress changes the date in year-end legislation.
